title: Micah's Homemade Shrine
overview: A man named Micah builds his own private place of worship, with a silver idol and a hired priest, showing how far Israel had drifted from its own laws.

parts.label: Stolen silver and a curse (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Micah had stolen a large sum of silver from his mother, then confessed after hearing her curse the thief, since curses were taken very seriously. His mother answers with a blessing, probably meant to cancel the curse now that it would fall on her own son.

parts.label: Silver made into an idol (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: She dedicates the silver to the LORD but uses it to make a carved and metal image, which Israel's law plainly forbade. She promised all of it but used only part, and it is unclear whether that shows stinginess or simply the cost of the work.

parts.label: A private shrine (v. 5)
parts.note: Micah adds an ephod (a priest's garment sometimes used to seek guidance from God) and household gods, small figures likely kept for protection or for guidance. He then makes his own son a priest, though the law reserved that role for one family descended from Aaron.

parts.label: No king in Israel (v. 6)
parts.note: The writer steps in to explain: with no central ruler, people made up their own rules. This line returns several times in the book's closing chapters as a judgment on the whole period.

parts.label: Hiring a wandering Levite (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: A young Levite, from the tribe set apart for religious service, leaves Bethlehem looking for somewhere to live, and Micah hires him for a yearly wage, clothing and food. Micah calls him 'father,' a title of respect for a religious guide, and formally installs him, something neither man had any right to do.

parts.label: Micah's confidence (v. 13)
parts.note: Micah assumes that having a proper Levite as his priest guarantees God's favor. The writer seems to mean this ironically, since everything around it breaks God's own instructions, and the next chapter shows how it turns out.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the book's repeated remark about there being no king mainly points ahead to Israel's human kings as the answer, or mainly faults the people for not treating God as their king.
think: What makes people feel sure they are doing the right thing, even when they are quietly making up the rules as they go?
